trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should argue that candidates stand out by doing the work before they are hired, not by sounding polished.
It should recommend concrete preparation such as bringing a plan, showing real understanding of the company, or demonstrating execution ability.
It should make the advice useful across roles while staying specific.
rubric_must_haves: Makes one core argument instead of listing generic interview tips.
Includes examples of what a standout candidate actually says or brings.
Applies to multiple seniority levels without becoming vague.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer says the best candidates separate themselves by proving they already think and act like owners. They research the company deeply, show where they would add value, and bring a concrete plan or analysis to the interview. The piece should stress that preparation and substance beat charisma, whether the role is SDR, AE, VP, or COO.
trace.prompt:
Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: How to Truly Stand Out in Any Job Interview, from SDR to COO

Style examples from train-owned source text.
Use them for voice only. They are not evidence for claims.
Do not copy long passages verbatim.
[Style 1]
Dear SaaStr: How Can You Ensure a Smooth Transition When A New Team Member Takes Over a Customer Account?
Add value in the first interaction.  This is so rare.
There’s nothing more frustrating than getting a random email, “Hi, Tony is gone from the company. I know nothing about you, but I’m your new rep. Can we schedule a call?”
Find some way to add value.
One great way is to demo upcoming features / an upcoming release.
“Hi, I’m Jason, your next account exec. I’d love to find a way to help even more. Can I show you or anyone on your team the new AI features we’re launching shortly? There’s no additional cost for them and based on what I can see, they may radically increase your efficiency.”
Not perfect. But much better.
A second, albeit riskier, way to add value is to set up a call asking for “honest feedback on how we’re doing.”
This works, too.  Customers often just want to be heard.  The “problem” is you might have to do something about it.
[Style 2]
Dear SaaStr: When Is It Too Soon to Target Enterprise Customers in SaaS?
It too soon to target enterprise clients when you can’t support their needs 90 days
after
you close them.
It’s sort of OK in the enterprise to promise features and functionality that are sort of there … so long as you deliver them fairly promptly after the deal closes.
In fact, it happens all the time. Enterprise customers will even sign contracts agreeing to buy so long as you implement a key feature with X number of days.
But if you don’t have the team, commitment and experience to deliver that functionality at least X days after you close a Big Customer … you aren’t ready.  They’ll churn or at least, never fully deploy.
You don’t have to have the full enterprise package in the early days to close enterprise customers, especially if they have interest in you.  You’ll get some slack as a new, emerging vendor.  Especially if you have a strong deployment team.
But you have to meet your commitments and promises to them fairly soon after the deal closes.

trace.answer:
How to Truly Stand Out in Any Job Interview, From SDR to CMO
We’ve talked a lot over the years on SaaStr about hiring great talent. And while hiring great folks is hard enough — once you hire someone, how do you make sure she succeeds? How does she truly stand out?
I think most candidates miss one simple thing. Especially junior ones.
They don’t really bring anything valuable to the table during the interview itself.
The best candidates almost always find a way to add real value in the first meeting.
And this doesn’t mean sending a fancy resume or covering letter. That’s table stakes today. No one reads those anymore anyway. We all expect resumes and cover letters to be top notch these days. Mediocre resumes and mediocre cover letters won’t advance you. Instead, they’ll mark you down immediately. If they bother reading it past the first few seconds.
No, instead, the best candidates somehow manage to bring some value, some insight, some learning to the table. Here’s how I would do it in different situations.
For example, in a Junior Sales Role like an SDR. What could you possibly say in a Zoom or coffee chat interview that adds any value? Well, I think two ideas work well:
First, ask for honest feedback on how they are doing today
. Most customers are happy to share candid thoughts on how things are going. Be careful here. Some may complain, which isn’t super helpful. Others may be brutally honest on why they don’t use your product yet. Still others may tell you exactly where you are winning against competitors. Whatever the case, having a chance to learn, share and listen will almost always create a bond between you. Even if you don’t end up working together.
Second, talk about how you can help them now
. Ask what pain points they are struggling with today, and figure out a way to solve one of them before the sale is closed.

Dear SaaStr: How Do I Build a Great SDR Team?
Building a great SDR team is one of the most critical steps in scaling a SaaS company, especially when you’re selling to the C-suite or enterprise. SDRs are the engine of your pipeline, and if you get this right, it can transform your sales organization.
Here’s how to do it:

1. Hire for “Fire in the Belly”
–
**What to Look For**
: SDRs don’t need prior experience in sales, but they need grit, hunger, and a relentless drive to succeed. Look for candidates who are coachable, curious, and have a strong work ethic. These traits are far more important than a polished resume.
–
**Pro Tip**
: Many great SDRs come from unconventional backgrounds—teachers, military veterans, or recent grads. They’re often looking for a career change and bring fresh perspectives.

7. Create a Career Path
– **Why?**: SDRs are often entry-level hires, and they’ll want to see a path forward. Without it, you’ll lose them to other companies.
– **What It Looks Like**:
SDR → Senior SDR → AE or other roles (e.g., Customer Success, Marketing)
Promote internally whenever possible. It’s less risky, and they already know your product and processes.
–
**Pro Tip**
: Highlight success stories of SDRs who’ve moved up in the company to inspire your team .
